Not likely. There a pros, such as the whole light speed thing, so "projectile" velocity per se is, well, light speed, which is pretty fast.

That doesn't stop huge ground-based lasers being useful. They can stop a missile. Well, lasers have limits. Today we've already reached close to their theoretical efficiency limit, so lasers won't really get that much smaller per watt of laser beam in the future.

We will need a completely new focused-energy-transfer technology if we want to get further. It will be in very, very, far future, and since we'll only be surviving for another 85ish years (until 2100), it is extremely unlikely.

missile makers will design missiles with random-path algorithms, which will bounce the missile around in flight. The US military, as far I know, haven't yet got anti-missile lasers to achieve this yet, but only successfully target a smoothly-flying missile, i.e. cruise missile.

You can point a laser beam WAY faster than you can change the direction of a missile. That would be ineffective, not to mention that it would waste a lot of propellant with all of the direction changes. The closed loop bandwidth of the laser tracking/targeting systems are in the kHz range, and the time constant of a missile velocity vector change is probably around 1Hz.

Using current technology it's possible to make a pretty lethal laser to fit inside a backpack, and with a hand held director. It would look a lot like the Ghostbusters backpack. Such a system would be only limited to ~1minute of laser operation before it needed to cool off, but you could start fires at a football field distance, and burn the shit out of things for that minute. It wouldn't blow holes in things, but it would nearly instantly catch any organic target on fire.
